01-feature-building.notes: All 22 pass the 5 hidden contract tests and their own suites (re-run locally). My differentiating probes found three real contract defects: I rejects valid input that repeats a dependency, raising a bogus cycle error with an empty ID list; G, H and R use recursive cycle diagnosis and raise RecursionError instead of ScheduleError for cycles of 1000 or more jobs (900 is fine); K and O deliberately reject whitespace-only ids, which is stricter than 'non-empty string', so I deducted a small amount. B is contract-correct but its ready selection is O(n^2), taking 4.5s at 5000 jobs and over 20s at 30000, so I penalised it under implementation quality. Cycle diagnostics that list the whole blocked set (cycle plus downstream) were accepted as meeting 'include the IDs involved when practical', with a small quality edge for concrete-cycle or SCC-member messages. Ties in score were broken as follows: C over M (simpler code for an equally precise result); M over N, Q and U (most thorough tests and the most precise diagnostic), then N (killed all 16 mutants); A over O (O's whitespace deviation); J over H (J is contract-correct, H is not); G over R (slightly broader tests). Caveat on the mutation numbers: several suites assert exact message text, so a mutant can 'survive' only because the matching test already fails on my reference. I judged those survivors by reading the test names and code rather than counting them against the suite. Rejecting malformed non-contract input (None depends_on, non-Job items, bad priority types) with ScheduleError rather than TypeError counted only toward implementation quality. Not verified: behaviour on Python versions other than the local 3.13.

03-infra-management.notes: Top three (R, C, O) are close. R and C are near-identical in config quality (fail-closed hex secrets, Redis auth, read-only proxy with minimal caps, runtime DNS). R ranks first on the runbook: it notes that unhealthy containers are not restarted and that single-file bind mounts need a restart, and it includes a restore rehearsal. O has the strongest verification (10 unit tests re-run OK) and non-root nginx and Redis, but it hard-codes a single-module app into the image and couples proxy health to DB readiness. Cross-cutting: no application source was supplied, so every API healthcheck either targets an assumed endpoint (graded on whether that assumption is stated; S used a TCP probe instead) or a stand-in app.py (D, J, K, O, T, U). B, P and Q have no .dockerignore with `COPY . .`, so .env is baked into the image, a real secret leak that caps their security score. Unverified (no daemon images, no starting containers): nginx -t, image builds and live healthchecks. T's read-only-nginx temp-path failure and N's local-scram backup failure are inferred from nginx and postgres-entrypoint behaviour, not observed. All 22 compose files rendered with `docker compose config` once dummy secrets were filled in. C, O, R, T and U intentionally fail on the unedited .env.example (empty required passwords). N's verify_config.py passes 69/69 but checks structure, not runbook commands.

06-product-planning.notes: OBJECTIVE_CHECKS.json was empty for every letter, so there were no process notes or automated checks. The grade rests on reading all 22 PLAN.md/RESPONSE.md pairs in full plus grep spot checks (encryption mentions, M0 presence, dates and staffing patterns). BRIEF.md and TASK.md were identical to the originals in every folder. Closest calls: (1) N vs L. Both purge before acceptance can occur, but N adds a proven submission-anchored cap with an interlock, a late-work path and scenario-linked ACs, so N leads. (2) B vs P, tied at 9.5. B has the more rigorous protocol, while P has the more defensible product call (purge at submission vs redefining 'accepted'). B is ranked first for its risk depth. (3) A vs C, tied at 8.75. C's risk analysis is deeper, but its acceptance barrier blocking indefinitely on lost tablets is a heavy product cost, so A is ahead. (4) U vs T at 7.5. T's TTL backstop can purge unsynced work, so U is ahead. (5) I vs F at 6.0. I is more complete but has invented schedule detail. Cross-cutting: the main differentiator was the 24-hour rule. Plans that purge at server-confirmed submission (L, P, E, N's Layer 2) or gate acceptance on purge (B by redefinition, C, D, U) handle the offline device. Plans that start the purge at the device's observation, or that wait until accepted_at+24h (F, G, I, J, M, O, S, T, V), are late by construction. H purges from sync time instead. 08-social-media.notes: All 22 submissions delivered SOCIAL.md and RESPONSE.md with no extra files; no process notes in OBJECTIVE_CHECKS.json. Counts were done with a section-splitting script (whitespace tokens and alnum-only words). Hard-limit failure: H's LinkedIn post is 115-117 words (<120) despite a header claiming 158. Borderlines: F Instagram is 79 alnum words without hashtags (83 with), and E's RESPONSE.md is 151 words including its heading (148 body). All Bluesky posts are 280 chars or fewer and all Bluesky replies are under 300. The main differentiator was invention: G, H and Q tell the commenter Japanese is supported, Q and J commit to lab seat arrangements, and several (E, H, L, P, G, Q) invent menus, log tools, emails or resumable indexing. Treating 'local processing, so no training' as an acceptable inference is a judgement call; replies that stated it were not penalised heavily. Very cautious submissions (C, M, R) score full factual marks but lose quality points because 'we don't have a confirmed training policy' and non-answers to the chatbot question would land badly in public. Closest calls: U vs T vs N (U's voice and discipline combined edged T, whose Bluesky copy is plainer; N lost a little for small invented colour) and the 7.5 cluster M/R/I/J, ordered by factual reliability. Platform conventions (e.g. Bluesky reply limits, Instagram line breaks) were judged from general knowledge; no network use.

10-general-operations.notes: No OBJECTIVE_CHECKS data for this task (all letters empty); grading is from reading the four deliverables against INBOX.md and hand-checking every time block for overlaps with the recurring meetings, Wed 13:00 unavailability, Sam's Wed 10:00-12:00 window, the 2h uninterrupted finance rule and lunch. Key discriminators: (1) whether the late-export path has a real 2h block (Tue afternoon if corrections land by ~14:00, then Thu 10:00-12:00 with zero slack; Wednesday cannot hold 2h around the rehearsal). D, J, R, S, G, M and F proposed blocks that are under 2h or that collide with the rehearsal or the Tue 16:00 meeting. (2) Whether the patch review lands early enough for non-Thursday QA. A put it on Thursday. (3) Treating the Wed 15:00 demo as a conflict for Product to decide, not a done deal. H, U, E and C handled this best; A, B, D and L declared it resolved. Close calls: U vs E (both near-complete; U's draft is tighter and its contradiction list includes the Wednesday-deploy reachability risk). I vs C at 9.0 (I's slip table is the most rigorous, C's draft is better; feasibility weight tipped it to I). G/O/K tie at 8.25, ordered by severity of their feasibility slips (G's Tue fallback overlaps the meeting; O misses the Tuesday fallback; K's fallback collides with its own change window and it assumes same-afternoon QA). P vs N at 7.5: P invents nothing, N invents Sam's Thursday availability. L vs R at 5.75: R has no viable fallback at all. Could not verify: actual QA or Sam availability, or whether the user must attend the demo. The inbox does not state these, so submissions were credited for asking rather than assuming.

12-frontend-editorial.notes:
K vs L (both 8.75) is the closest call: L is equally polished, but K's submerged-'Water'-plus-riverbed motif answers the 'one strong display motif' brief more directly, and L has 8px microtype. F, M, C and G tie at 8.5. The tie-break is taste, then bugs: F has no defects; C loses on the mobile '
' word-join; G's desktop hero is left-heavy. Reading mode: a palette swap (B, D, F, I, K, M, N, S, U, V) was accepted as functional, but one-column or enlarged-type reading views (C, G, H, J, O, P) earned more credit. Bugs reproduced in my own harness: N loses the first click (layout shift on blur), I wipes its success on Enter-key submit, J shows a hidden success card on load, B/K do not announce email errors, D lacks aria-invalid/describedby, and U/A hide text in reading mode. B, H, M, O, T and U use scroll-reveal; I re-captured them after scrolling so the hidden content was judged fairly. 13-frontend-playful.notes: Top three are close: D edges C and K on the most useful all-done (water forecast), add-observation, and a detail view covering light/water/history. C has the boldest, best-composed three-column desktop. K has the clearest prioritisation copy and a clever rhythm with missed and catch-up days. C ranks above K on desktop composition at equal totals. A vs U (8.25 each): A ranks first for keyboard shortcuts and more complete household summaries. Among the 7.75s, B ranks first for polish despite its invisible primary focus ring and 'Watered' mislabels, then E (visual defects and overflow at 1024), F (hero-first desktop, 8-9 px text), and L (320 px overflow). M and N are both badly broken: N's flows work by mouse inside a modal but its weekly chart and labels are broken, while M can't be used with a pointer at all because its shortcuts overlay never closes. Process notes: A was a medium-effort re-run and I a low-effort re-run; neither changes the grading of the delivered files. Not verified: screen-reader output beyond the accessible names and live-region text I read, and colour-contrast ratios (judged visually). Focus rings were checked by the computed outline/box-shadow on each tab stop plus a focused-button montage (out/focus-montage.png). The probe's generic 'complete all' loop gave false negatives for E, I, J, N, O, R and S; each was re-tested by hand with t.js and the scores use the manual results.
